growth_story.headline: Logs, conflict and now gold: income per person in the Solomon Islands is still 20.5 percent below its 1995 peak, and below its 1980 level.
growth_story.arc: Income per person in the Solomon Islands peaked in 1995 and in 2025 was still 20.5 percent below that peak, and lower than in 1980, the first year of the record. From 1990 to 1997 it grew 2.4 percent a year on a logging boom that, the World Bank says, ended with the Asian financial crisis in 1997. From 1998 to 2005 it shrank 2.4 percent a year: ethnic conflict, known as the Tensions, brought a collapse of government, with falls of 16.2 percent in 2000 and 9.7 percent in 2001, until a regional peace mission helped end the fighting in 2003. From 2006 to 2013 growth came back at 2.5 percent a year, carried by logging at rates far above what the forests can sustain, by aid and by public spending. Since 2014 income per person has fallen 1.3 percent a year, first as a short restart of the Gold Ridge mine faded, and later as logging shrank and the pandemic and the 2022 fuel price shock brought three years of contraction from 2020 to 2022. Growth turned positive again in 2023, 2024 and 2025, at 0.4, 0.6 and 1.2 percent, led by a surge in gold mining.

threads.title: The logging boom and its end
threads.text: Growth in the early 1990s was rapid but uneven, driven mostly by logging. The World Bank links the end of that boom to the Asian financial crisis of 1997, which set off a fiscal crisis and cut the logging rents that had funded politicians and their supporters. The era of shrinking income per person began in 1998.

threads.title: The Tensions, 1998 to 2003
threads.text: From 1998 a conflict between ethnic groups over land and economic grievances broke down government and stopped much of the market economy, including the Gold Ridge mine. An Australian-led regional mission helped end the fighting in 2003.

threads.title: Post-conflict growth on logs and aid
threads.text: The recovery after 2003 leaned on logging at rates well above the sustainable yield, on large aid flows and on a bigger public sector. A short restart of the Gold Ridge mine added to growth in 2011 and 2012 and then pulled it down in 2013 and 2014, as the 2006 to 2013 era gave way to decline.

threads.title: From logs to gold
threads.text: Logging, long the main export, is shrinking, and gold from the reopened Gold Ridge mine now leads exports and growth. The World Bank describes this as a shift from one extractive sector to another, with mining creating far fewer jobs than logging did. The IMF lists declining logging, a narrow economy and weak governance as limits on growth.

threads.title: Pandemic, unrest and rising debt
threads.text: Civil unrest, the pandemic and the 2022 fuel price shock hit the economy, and income per person fell in 2020, 2021 and 2022, leaving the economy below its earlier path. Public debt has climbed sharply since before the pandemic.

since_last_year.text: In 2026 two new shocks hit a narrow rebound that the World Bank calls fragile. The war in the Middle East pushed up the price of imported fuel, on which the country depends almost entirely, and Cyclone Maila struck in April. Both the World Bank and the IMF expect growth to slow in 2026.

growth_story.tension: The sources tell of a gold-led rebound, with mining now the engine of growth, but income per person grew only 0.4, 0.6 and 1.2 percent in 2023, 2024 and 2025 and in 2025 was still below its 2019 level. Population growth takes up much of the growth in total output, as the MCC analysis already noted for the years before the pandemic, so a recovery that looks real in the economy as a whole is barely visible per person.
